title: Selective undo & intrusion recovery prior art (Retro, Warp, Aire)
outcome: Know which selective-undo mechanisms (action history graph, dependency tracking, selective re-execution) transfer to an LLM agent network and where they break
acceptance: ≥5 primary sources with URLs, including Retro (OSDI'10) and Warp (SOSP'11) papers
Table comparing ≥4 systems on: what is recorded, how dependencies are tracked, how legitimate work is preserved, handling of non-determinism, overhead
Explicit analysis of what breaks when the 're-executed' actor is a non-deterministic LLM agent
'Implications for our design' section naming the minimal dependency data our Recorder must capture
summary:
Retro (OSDI'10), Warp (SOSP'11), Aire (SOSP'13, not OSDI'14) and Taser (SOSP'05) all undo one actor's damage while keeping later legitimate work, via a recorded dependency graph + taint + selective rollback/re-execution. Hypothesis H1 half holds: graph and selective rollback transfer; replay-based re-execution does not, since LLM agents are non-deterministic (Warp/Aire rely on recording non-determinism; Taser/Retro sidestep it).
All systems hit external effects and pause for a human or send a compensating message (link to RES-02). Aire's authorized-repair model is the relevant precedent for who may trigger undo. Taser's separate log backend is the precedent for logs agents cannot edit.
Top design implication: Recorder must store per action: agent_id + delegation/authority, write set with before/after hashes, READ SET WITH VERSIONS READ (incl. other agents' outputs), message IDs on both sides, effect class. Recovery = taint forward, revert tainted versions, hand work back to agents to re-plan with approval; do not replay LLMs.
Caveats: GoEx read at abstract level only; Retro venue not shown in fetched PDF; numbers extracted via fetch tool, spot-check.
